entry.title: From chatbot to coworker: three years of LLMs in hydrology

link.title: From chatbot to coworker: three years of LLMs in hydrology

entry.content:
In September 2023, Water Resources Research published an editorial by Foroumandi and colleagues titled “ChatGPT in Hydrology and Earth Sciences: Opportunities, Prospects, and Concerns.” It was one of the first careful attempts by our community to say what these tools were good for and where they should be kept away. Three years and several model generations later, it is worth reading again next to two recent hydrology papers and Christopher Summerfield’s book These Strange New Minds. Together they show how quickly the question has changed: from “can it write a correct loop?” to “can it run a 531-basin experiment overnight, and should we let it?”

2023: a useful but unreliable writing partner

The 2023 editorial was balanced, and most of its observations held up. ChatGPT was good at beginner-to-intermediate coding (reading and cleaning data, explaining syntax, translating between languages, adding comments), at polishing prose for non-native writers, and at summarizing text. The problems began with anything harder:

  • Complex code. In one test, after several rounds of error messages, the model “fixed” a shape mismatch in a deep-learning script by inserting an array of zeros. The code ran, and the answer was meaningless.
  • Unstable physics. Asked how shortwave radiation affects precipitation in humid regions, it gave one plausible explanation, then reversed itself as soon as the authors said it was wrong.
  • Invented references. All three citations it supplied for that answer turned out not to exist.
  • Arguing a bad case. When asked to help convince a reviewer that an uncalibrated model was valid, it obliged with persuasive talking points.
  • Frozen knowledge. It had no internet access and knew nothing after its training cutoff.

The authors’ conclusion was that ChatGPT was a compiler rather than an author, and their recommendations followed from that: never use it as the sole source of information, disclose its use, keep teaching programming so researchers can check AI-written code, and redesign assignments around critical thinking. One recommendation aged badly. AI-text detectors were suggested for screening manuscripts, but they proved unreliable; OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 because of low accuracy. The rest still reads as sound advice, and some of it has become more important, not less.

What changed: from answering to acting

The biggest change since 2023 is not that models know more hydrology, although they do. It is that they can now act. Current assistants search the web, read and write files, run code, see the errors, and try again. Open standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) let a model call external tools in a structured way. “Agentic” coding tools can take a goal, plan the steps, edit a whole project and test the result with little hand-holding. I built this website that way, by describing what I wanted and reviewing what came back.

The market has changed too. ChatGPT is now one of many: Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen and Moonshot’s Kimi compete closely, and several strong models have openly released weights. Competition has moved from raw capability toward cost. By one industry index, frontier token prices in late 2026 are about 85% below their March 2023 level, and open-weight models are typically far cheaper than proprietary ones, although the newest frontier models have become more expensive again over the past year. For agents, which can consume more than a million tokens per task, cost per task now matters as much as cost per token.

The figure below summarizes how the role of the LLM has shifted across the three hydrology papers discussed here.

Figure 1. How the role of the LLM changed across three studies. In 2023 the human did all the running and checking. In the GRL study, the LLM proposed parameters inside a loop built by the researchers. In the Journal of Hydrology study, agents planned, coded, ran and debugged entire modelling workflows within an expert-designed process. Original schematic by Daeha Kim, based on Foroumandi et al. (2023), Zhu et al. (2026) and Li et al. (2026).

2025: the LLM inside the calibration loop

Zhu et al. (2026, Geophysical Research Letters) asked whether an LLM could replace the optimization algorithm in calibrating the VIC model for a sub-basin of the Yangtze. Judging from the models tested (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3 and two Llama models) and the submission date of October 2025, the experiments reflect LLMs of roughly mid-2025. The researchers wrote a Python program that ran VIC, computed NSE, RMSE and bias, and sent the results and hydrograph to the LLM, which proposed the next parameter set. The LLM never ran or imitated the model; it only made the decisions that SCE-UA or NSGA-III would normally make.

The result was mixed in an informative way. DeepSeek-R1 reached an NSE of about 0.89 within roughly 200 iterations and matched SCE-UA’s best NSE using fewer model runs. It also focused early on the parameters hydrologists know to be sensitive, such as infiltration shape and soil depth. The other four models did worse than the standard algorithms. One basin, one model and six parameters is a small test, and “fewer iterations” says nothing about API cost or about whether the result repeats on a second run. But it showed that a reasoning model could act like a sensible, if inexperienced, calibrator.

2026: agents that build the whole workflow

Li et al. (2026, Journal of Hydrology), submitted in May 2026, used the next generation of models: GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen-Plus. Their system, HydroAIM, uses several cooperating agents connected through MCP. Given a task, the agents prepare the data, write and run the training code, read the error messages, fix them and evaluate the result, all without a human in the loop.

Three findings stand out.

  • It works most of the time. Across 125 modelling tasks with five different LLMs, 92.8% of runs succeeded. On 531 CAMELS basins, the agent-built models reached a median NSE of 0.58 for basin-by-basin LSTMs (close to the 0.61 of the calibrated SAC-SMA benchmark) and 0.73 for a single LSTM trained on all basins, which is in line with published LSTM benchmarks.
  • Planning, not knowledge, is the bottleneck. When the researchers removed the expert-designed workflow and let the agents organize the task themselves, the success rate fell to 0%. Agents declared victory after one sub-step, looped on the same tool calls, or lost track of file paths after their context was summarized.
  • Experts are still needed. In one run, weak performance turned out to come from a data-loading error that withheld same-day weather inputs. When prompts pushed the agents toward “bigger” architectures, they switched to models that performed worse. Newer versions of some models also had to be used partway through the study, which makes exact reproduction harder.

The cost appendix of the same paper makes the price competition concrete. A successful end-to-end run used between half a million and two million tokens, and the price of that run differed by a factor of 25 to 45 depending on the model, even though all five models completed the tasks at similar rates.

Figure 2. API cost of one representative successful run for each LLM and each of five task types. Data from Table A1 of Li et al. (2026); plotted by Daeha Kim. Costs reflect list prices at the time of the study and will change.

Checking a book’s predictions

Christopher Summerfield, a cognitive neuroscientist, wrote These Strange New Minds in 2024. His closing chapter makes a few claims that are easy to check against what has happened since.

He argued that LLMs are not minds like ours: they have no body, no friends and no motivation of their own, and so no built-in curiosity about the world. Nothing in the papers above contradicts that. In both studies, the question, the data, the success criterion and the judgement of what counts as physically plausible all came from people.

He identified two engineering limits, short memory and weak long-term planning, and expected both to be solved soon. That has partly happened. Assistants now remember across conversations and agents routinely complete multi-step tasks. But the 0% result without an expert workflow shows that open-ended, long-horizon scientific work still breaks down unless someone gives the agent a structure to follow.

He predicted that we would drift gradually toward AI that acts rather than merely answers, starting with simple, well-defined tasks. That is exactly the path we have seen. Software was first, because code can be run and tested automatically. Scientific modelling, with its many judgement calls, is following more slowly.

He also cited early evidence that AI help lifts the least-skilled workers the most and could act as a leveller. In research, the early picture points the other way. In a 2026 survey of 1,260 social scientists, 81% had used AI chatbots for research, but only 20% used coding agents weekly. Use was concentrated among economists, doctoral students and researchers at top universities. That sample was self-selected, so the true share is probably lower, and I know of no equivalent survey for hydrology. My impression matches it: agentic workflows are still rare in our field.

Finally, he warned that forecasts about AI replacing professionals have often been wrong. His example was the 2016 prediction that we would soon stop training radiologists, which has not come true. The hydrology papers suggest a similar story for us. The agents did not replace the hydrologist; they moved the hydrologist’s work from writing code to designing workflows, checking assumptions and judging results.

Why most research has not switched yet

Agentic tools have spread quickly in software development but slowly in research. I think the reasons are specific to science.

  • Verification costs time. A program that runs is not a program that is right. The zero-array “fix” from 2023 and the missing-forcing bug from 2026 are the same kind of error at different scales.
  • Reproducibility is harder. The same prompt can give different code from day to day, and model versions change underneath you. Li et al. recommend recording model identifiers, prompts, tool definitions and execution logs; few groups do this yet.
  • Costs are real. A single agentic run is cheap, but sensitivity analyses across hundreds of basins add up, and frontier models can cost tens of times more than open ones.
  • You still need to know the craft. To supervise an agent, you need enough coding and enough hydrology to recognize a wrong answer. Ironically, this keeps the people who would benefit most from the tools from trusting them.

What I tell students now

The 2023 editorial ended with the advice to use AI as a tool for problem-solving, but never to let it solve the problem by itself. In 2026 I would phrase it slightly differently: treat the agent as a fast, tireless junior colleague whose work you must check.

  • Do let agents handle the plumbing: downloading data, reformatting files, plotting, writing tests and rerunning experiments.
  • Do use them to run more checks than you could by hand, such as sensitivity tests, additional basins or alternative model structures.
  • Do not let them choose your research question, your success criterion or your interpretation of the physics.
  • Do not report a number you cannot reproduce. Record the model and version, the prompt and the code that was actually run.
  • Keep learning to code and keep learning hydrology. In 2023 that was needed to fix the AI’s mistakes. In 2026 it is needed to notice them.

Questions to think about

  1. The GRL study accepted parameter sets based on NSE alone. What could go wrong if an agent optimizes only one metric for you?
  2. Why might an agent that cannot plan on its own still succeed when given an expert workflow? What does that suggest about the value of writing down your own modelling procedures?
  3. If a cheap model and an expensive model both succeed 90% of the time, what else would you want to know before choosing one for a 500-basin study?

한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 2023년 WRR editorial은 ChatGPT를 저자가 아니라 편집 도구로 보고, 복잡한 코드, 물리적 설명, 인용에서 믿을 수 없다고 경고했다. 그로부터 3년이 지난 2026년 10월 현재, LLM은 보정(calibration) 루프 안에서 직접 매개변수를 결정하고(GRL), 여러 에이전트가 531개 유역의 LSTM 모형을 처음부터 끝까지 만들어 낼 정도로 발전했다(J. Hydrol.). 하지만 전문가가 직접 설계한 절차가 없으면 성공률은 0%로 떨어졌고, 데이터 오류를 잡아낸 것도 여전히 사람이었다. 연구 현장에서 LLM을 에이전트 방식으로 사용하는 경우가 아직 드문 이유는 검증, 재현성, 비용, 그리고 결과를 판단할 전문성 때문이다. 에이전트 방식의 사용은 앞으로 늘어나겠지만, 학생들에게 필요한 것이 코딩과 수문학에 대한 탄탄한 이해라는 사실은 변함이 없다. 바다 위에서 정확한 방향을 잡도록 도와주는 것은 출렁거리는 파도가 아니라 위치가 변하지 않는 북극성이다.

References

Foroumandi, E., Moradkhani, H., Sanchez-Vila, X., Singha, K., Castelletti, A., & Destouni, G. (2023). ChatGPT in hydrology and Earth sciences: Opportunities, prospects, and concerns. Water Resources Research, 59, e2023WR036288. https://doi.org/10.1029/2023WR036288

Zhu, Z., Tang, Y., Tang, X., et al. (2026). Large language models as calibration agents in hydrological modeling: Feasibility and limitations. Geophysical Research Letters, 53, e2025GL120043. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL120043

Li, Y., Hu, S., Zhang, F., et al. (2026). Grounding large language models in hydrologic modelling. Journal of Hydrology, 679, 136358. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2026.136358

Summerfield, C. (2025). These Strange New Minds: How AI Learned to Talk and What It Means.

Lyttelton, Massenkoff & Wilmers (2026). Coding agents in the social sciences. Anthropic. https://www.anthropic.com/research/coding-agents-social-sciences

BenchLM (2026). LLM pricing statistics. https://benchlm.ai/stats/llm-pricing

Both figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1 and Figure 2.
entry.summary: Re-reading a 2023 editorial on ChatGPT in hydrology next to two new papers and a book on AI: what LLMs could not do then, what agents can do now, and why most research has not switched yet.

entry.title: Approaching 1.5°C from above
entry.content:
For most of my career, 1.5°C was a line we were trying not to cross. That framing is about to expire. Human-induced warming is now close to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels and rising by roughly a quarter of a degree per decade. The United Nations Environment Programme’s new report, Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return (UNEP 2026), starts from a blunt premise: 1.5°C will be exceeded within the next few years. The question is no longer whether we cross it, but how far past it we go, how long we stay there, and whether we can come back.

The report’s short answer is that the goal stays the same, but we now have to approach it from above. Here are the messages I think matter most, followed by what they mean for those of us who design and manage water systems.

1. Overshoot is a pathway with stages, not a single event

The report describes an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway in four stages: exceedance (warming passes 1.5°C), peak (warming stops rising once net CO₂ emissions reach zero), decline (warming falls slowly, only if the world removes more CO₂ than it emits for decades), and stabilization. Matching these, it proposes three overlapping response phases:

  • Immediate response: cut emissions fast, especially methane and other short-lived pollutants, and protect the most vulnerable people and ecosystems now.
  • Coping and containment: reach at least net-zero emissions to stop the rise, and manage severe impacts while temperatures peak.
  • Long-term resilience: sustain net-negative CO₂ emissions to bring temperatures down, and adapt where losses have become permanent.

The report stresses that this is not a preferred or acceptable pathway. It is simply the best option still on the table. There are no benign scenarios above 1.5°C.

2. Every five years of delay adds about 0.1°C to the peak

The most quantitative message is also the simplest. Warming scales almost linearly with cumulative CO₂ emissions, so the peak temperature is set by how much CO₂ we emit before reaching net zero. The report puts the remaining budget for a 50% chance of 1.5°C at only about 130 GtCO₂ from 2026, against current emissions of about 40 GtCO₂ per year. At that rate the budget is gone in roughly three years. Staying within it would require emissions to fall in a straight line to zero in just over six years.

Because about 220 GtCO₂ produces 0.1°C of warming (the IPCC best estimate), every five years of emissions at today’s level adds roughly 0.1°C to whatever peak we eventually reach. The figure below is my own back-of-the-envelope version of that arithmetic. It is not a figure from the report.

Figure. (a) Three idealized CO₂ pathways that all take 30 years to fall from 40 GtCO₂ per year to net zero, starting in 2026, 2031 or 2036. The dashed line is what staying within the 1.5°C budget would require. (b) The resulting peak warming, computed as 1.5°C plus the warming from CO₂ emitted beyond the 130 GtCO₂ budget, using the IPCC AR6 transient climate response to cumulative emissions (best estimate 0.45°C per 1000 GtCO₂; bars show the likely range of 0.27–0.63). Non-CO₂ gases and CO₂ removal are held fixed, so this is an illustration of the budget logic, not a projection. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported in UNEP (2026).

Even the prompt-start case peaks at about 1.7°C. That is consistent with the report’s estimate that full implementation of every current national pledge and net-zero target still implies a peak of around 1.8°C. Each delay of five years pushes the peak up by another tenth of a degree.

3. Coming back down is slow, limited and uncertain

Returning below 1.5°C requires the world to become net-negative: removing more CO₂ than it emits, for decades. The report is sober about how hard that is:

  • Even optimistic scaling of carbon dioxide removal is unlikely to lower temperatures by more than a few tenths of a degree this century.
  • At today’s scale, afforestation and forest management would take over a century to reverse just 0.1°C of warming, and that assumes zero residual CO₂ emissions.
  • Geological storage is finite. Merely maintaining net-zero CO₂ could use up the estimated storage capacity of sedimentary basins by around 2200.
  • Once the peak exceeds about 1.8°C, a return to 1.5°C within this century becomes increasingly difficult.

The conclusion is that removal is needed in addition to deep emission cuts, never instead of them. The cheapest tenth of a degree is the one we never emit.

4. Some damage does not reverse when the temperature does

Bringing temperatures down helps, but the climate system has long memory. Glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass by 2100, and glacier loss will continue for centuries even if warming stabilizes. Sea level keeps rising long after the peak. Even so, a pathway that declines rather than stabilizing at a higher level could reduce sea-level rise by almost half a metre by 2300. Species extinctions and some ecosystem shifts, such as the loss of coral reefs, may not be undone at all. The report’s message to decision-makers is that the legacy of the peak is inherited by every stage that follows.

What this means for water

Reading the report as a hydrologist, three points stand out.

Our design assumptions have a new shape. Almost twenty years ago, Milly and colleagues argued that “stationarity is dead,” meaning that we can no longer design water infrastructure as if the past climate will repeat. Overshoot adds a twist. The climate we design for is not just moving. It may rise, peak and then partly fall within the lifetime of a single dam, levee or water supply system. A reservoir rule curve or design flood that is right for the peak may be wrong for the decline. The report explicitly calls for infrastructure that favours robustness and safety margins over optimization, and for forward-looking stress tests instead of planning from the historical record.

Water availability can change non-linearly. In glacier-fed basins, meltwater first rises as glaciers shrink, then falls as they disappear. A study cited in the report suggests that if temperatures decline after the peak and glaciers partly regrow, downstream runoff could drop further still, into what the authors call “trough water.” For communities that rely on seasonal meltwater, the decline stage is not automatically a recovery.

Adaptation has to be iterative. Because the path, the peak and the timing are all uncertain, the report argues that adaptation must be revisited repeatedly rather than designed once. This is the reasoning behind the decision-centric and scenario-neutral approaches my group has used to assess dams and river basins: start from the thresholds at which a system fails, then ask how plausible those conditions are under many possible futures, instead of betting on a single projection.

The bottom line

The report closes on a point worth repeating: overshoot is an argument for urgency, not resignation. Every fraction of a degree avoided and every year by which overshoot is shortened reduces risk to people, ecosystems and the infrastructure we build. For students thinking about a career in hydrology and water resources, this is the problem your generation will manage: water systems built for one climate, operated through another and possibly handed on in a third.

Questions to think about

  1. If a 100-year design flood is estimated for the peak-warming period, how should it be revised during the decline stage?
  2. Which water infrastructure in Korea has a design life that will span exceedance, peak and decline?
  3. Using the budget arithmetic in the figure, how much later could emissions start to fall if the target were a 1.8°C peak instead?

Reference

United Nations Environment Programme (2026). Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return. Nairobi. https://doi.org/10.59117/20.500.11822/49857

Milly, P. C. D., et al. (2008). Stationarity is dead: Whither water management? Science, 319, 573–574. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1151915

entry.summary: What UNEP's Limiting Overshoot report says about exceeding 1.5°C, why every five years of delay costs about 0.1°C, and what a temperature that rises and then falls means for water engineering.
